extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in partial differential equations, especially hyperbolic conservation laws
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, selection criteria, and equivalent formulations used to define/identify physically correct weak solutions of scalar and system conservation laws (entropy pairs, vanishing viscosity, kinetic formulations, limits). Includes criteria for uniqueness, admissible shocks, and asymptotic limits (hydrodynamical and diffusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral (weak) solution (scalar)
rubrics_metrics.description: u ∈ L1_loc(Rn × (0,∞)) is an integral solution of ut + div F(u) = 0 with u(·,0)=g provided the integral identity holds: ∫_0^∞ ∫_{Rn} (u v_t + F(u) · Dv) dx dt + ∫_{Rn} g v(·,0) dx = 0 for all v ∈ C^1_c(Rn × [0,∞)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the natural weak formulation but alone is inadequate to single out the physically correct solution (discontinuous integral solutions can be nonphysical). The initial datum g is taken in L1_loc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entropy/entropy-flux pair (scalar)
rubrics_metrics.description: A pair (Φ, Ψ) is an entropy/entropy-flux pair for ut + div F(u)=0 if (i) Φ: R → R is convex and (ii) Ψ: R → R^n satisfies DΨ = b Φ' where b = F'. Equivalently Ψ_i(z) = ∫_0^z b_i(v) Φ'(v) dv up to additive constants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If u is C^1 then Φ(u)_t + div Ψ(u) = 0; the pair is used to measure entropy production where u is not smooth. The convexity of Φ is essential to obtain inequalities from viscous approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entropy solution (scalar)
rubrics_metrics.description: u ∈ C([0,∞); L1(Rn)) is an entropy solution of ut + div F(u)=0, u(·,0)=g if for every entropy pair (Φ,Ψ) the inequality Φ(u)_t + div Ψ(u) ≤ 0 holds in the weak sense (i.e. the integral inequality (16) holds for all nonnegative test functions v), and u(·,0)=g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This inequality selects the physically correct weak solution (e.g. rules out nonphysical shocks). Motivation and justification come from the vanishing viscosity limit uε solving uε_t + div F(uε) = ε Δ uε and passing to the limit as ε→0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing viscosity selection principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularize the conservation law by adding viscosity: uε_t + div F(uε) = ε Δ uε with ε>0; smooth solutions uε exist and, under suitable estimates and convergence uε → u (boundedly a.e. or locally uniformly), the limit u satisfies entropy inequalities Φ(u)_t + div Ψ(u) ≤ 0 for all entropy pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used to motivate and justify the entropy condition: physically correct shocks arise as ε→0 limits of viscous problems while nonphysical shocks cannot be limits. Technical hypotheses (bounds on ε|Duε|^2, sup bounds, etc.) are required to pass to the limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kruzkov L1-contraction / uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: If u and û are entropy solutions of the same scalar conservation law with initial data g and ĝ respectively, then for each 0 ≤ s ≤ t one has ||u(·,t) - û(·,t)||_{L1(Rn)} ≤ ||u(·,s) - û(·,s)||_{L1(Rn)}. In particular, an entropy solution is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the fundamental uniqueness/stability result for scalar entropy solutions; consult Kruzkov for proof and hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral solution (system)
rubrics_metrics.description: For system ut + div F(u) = 0 with u : Rn×[0,∞)→Rm, u is an integral solution if ∫_0^∞ ∫_{Rn} (u · v_t + F(u) : Dv) dx dt + ∫_{Rn} g · v(·,0) dx = 0 for all v ∈ C^1_c(Rn × [0,∞); Rm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vector-valued analogue of the scalar weak formulation; again insufficient alone to determine physical admissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entropy/entropy-flux pair (systems)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a system (1) with B = DF, (Φ,Ψ) is an entropy/entropy-flux pair if (i) Φ: R^m → R is convex and (ii) Ψ: R^m → R^n satisfies DΨ = B DΦ (componentwise: Ψ_i_{z_k} = Σ_l (∂F^l_i/∂z_k) Φ_{z_l}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Φ,Ψ exist they give conserved quantities for smooth solutions: Φ(u)_t + div Ψ(u) = 0. For general systems such pairs may not exist; for physically derived systems one often expects some.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rankine–Hugoniot jump condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Across a smooth shock curve x = s(t) separating left state u_l and right state u_r, the shock speed satisfies ˙s (u_r - u_l) = F(u_r) - F(u_l).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derived from the weak form of the PDE in regions where u is piecewise smooth; necessary condition for any discontinuity (shock or contact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oleinik condition E (admissibility for shocks in 1D)
rubrics_metrics.description: For u_l < u_r the condition is F(u) ≥ F(u_r) + (F(u_r)-F(u_l))/(u_r-u_l) (u between u_l and u_r), equivalently the graph of F over [u_l,u_r] lies above the chord joining (u_l,F(u_l)) and (u_r,F(u_r)). For u_l > u_r the reverse inequality holds. These inequalities are called Oleinik's condition E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condition E ensures characteristics can collide with the shock but cannot emanate from it (geometric irreversibility). Consequences: if F is strictly convex then u_l ≥ u_r, if strictly concave u_l ≤ u_r. This provides a single-sided monotonicity admissibility criterion that rules out nonphysical shocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entropy inequality across shocks (jump form)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any entropy pair (Φ,Ψ) and shock curve with normal ν, one obtains the jump inequality ˙s(Φ(u_r)-Φ(u_l)) ≥ Ψ(u_r)-Ψ(u_l) (equivalently the integrated form (30)), which combined with Rankine–Hugoniot yields the Oleinik inequalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the localized version of the entropy inequality that constrains admissible jumps; taking special Φ (e.g. ±identity) recovers Rankine–Hugoniot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinetic formulation (scalar): representation via w and m
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists w(x,y,t) and a nonnegative Radon measure m on Rn×R×(0,∞) such that wt + b(y)·Dx w = ∂_y m in distributions, w(x,y,t) = χ_{u(x,t)}(y) (the pseudo-Maxwellian) and u(x,t) = ∫ w(x,y,t) dy. Here b = F'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The kinetic equation is equivalent to the scalar entropy formulation: m encodes the family of entropy dissipation measures simultaneously. The construction and equivalence require bounds (w bounded, compact y-support depending on ||u||_∞) and are proved via testing with v(x,t)Φ'(y)ψ(y) and passing to limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-Maxwellian χ_a(y)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each parameter a ∈ R define χ_a(y) = 1 if 0 < y ≤ a; χ_a(y) = -1 if a ≤ y ≤ 0; χ_a(y) = 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: χ_a is the mesoscopic profile used in the kinetic representation w = χ_{u(x,t)}(y); it encodes the macroscopic value a as a structured y-distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entropy production measure γ_Φ
rubrics_metrics.description: For each entropy pair (Φ,Ψ) one may represent Φ(u)_t + div Ψ(u) = -γ_Φ in the distribution sense, where γ_Φ is a nonnegative Radon measure supported where u fails to be C^1 (e.g. shocks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: γ_Φ records entropy dissipation along shocks and non-smooth regions; the kinetic measure m simultaneously records the γ_Φ for all Φ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrodynamical limit (from scaled kinetic to conservation law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the scaled kinetic equation wε_t + b(y)·Dx wε = (1/ε)(χ_{uε} - wε) with uε = ∫ wε dy and initial wε = χ_g. Under uniform bounds (|wε| ≤ 1, sign on y≥0 etc.), compactness of {uε} in L1_loc, decomposition (1/ε)(χ_{uε} - wε) = ∂_y mε with mε ≥ 0 and L1 bound supε ∫ mε < ∞, one extracts a limit w = χ_u and u the unique entropy solution of ut + div F(u)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a rigorous derivation of the scalar conservation law as the hydrodynamical limit of the kinetic equation; key steps: show mε nonnegative, bound its total mass, use compactness to pass to limit in the kinetic equation and identify w = χ_u.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak entropy function for isentropic Euler (construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A weak entropy Φ(ρ,v) for the isentropic Euler system satisfies the linear PDE Φ_{ρρ} = (p'(ρ)/ρ^2) Φ_{vv} (ρ>0) (equation (18)) with initial conditions Φ = 0, Φ_ρ = g(v) on ρ>0 for given g. The associated flux Ψ is computed from relations Ψ_ρ = v Φ_ρ + (p'(ρ)/ρ) Φ_v and Ψ_v = ρ Φ_ρ + v Φ_v.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing g(v)=v^2 yields the physical energy entropy; convexity of Φ in variables (ρ,ρv) is related to convexity of g. These entropies feed into the kinetic formulation for Euler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinetic formulation for Euler (one-dim)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Euler entropy solution (ρ,ρv) is equivalent to existence of w(x,y,t)=χ(ρ,y-v) and a (nonpositive) measure m such that wt + [(θ y + (1-θ)v) w]_x = ∂_y^2 M (represented as m) in distributions, with θ = (γ-1)/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This kinetic formulation parallels the scalar case and hinges on representation of weak entropies Φ(ρ,v) = ∫ g(y) χ(ρ,y-v) dy; the measure encodes entropy dissipation and finite-energy bounds control integrability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffusion limit: structural hypotheses and construction of diffusion coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: For the linear transport-coupling system wε_t + (1/ε) B D wε = (1/ε^2) C wε with B = diag(b_k) and coupling matrix C, assume (i) c_{kl}>0 for k≠l and Σ_l c_{kl}=0 (row sums zero), (ii) by Perron–Frobenius there is a unique positive probability vector π with C^T π = 0, and (iii) average velocity balance Σ_k π_k b_k = 0. Then for each coordinate j there exists a unique d_j with C d_j = -b_j and d_j · 11 = 0, and the diffusion coefficients are a_{ij} = Σ_k π_k b_k^i d_k^j; the resulting matrix A is nonnegative definite and the limit u solves u_t - Σ_{i,j} a_{ij} u_{x_i x_j} = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These algebraic structural hypotheses are the admissibility/compatibility conditions ensuring that as ε→0 each component w_{k,ε} converges to the same scalar u and that the macroscopic limit is a diffusion equation. The Perron–Frobenius theory and the solvability/normalization of C d_j = -b_j are essential steps.
